s: What was the original name of Mumtaz Mahal?
x: Mumtaz Mahal, born Arjumand Banu Begum, was Asaf Khan's daughter and is entombed in the Taj Mahal.

s: Whose eldest son was Dara Shikoh?
x: Dara Shikoh was Shah Jahan's eldest son; Jahangir's son was Khusrau.

s: Who among the following was the Hindu mother of Shah Jahan and the wife of Jahangir?
x: Jagat Gosain was a Hindu wife of Jahangir and the mother of Shah Jahan.

s: Which of the following pairs (Emperor – son) is correctly matched?
x: Murad was Shah Jahan's son; Kamran was Babur's and Khusrau Jahangir's.

s: Which of the following texts was translated into Persian by Dara Shikoh?
x: Dara Shikoh translated the Bhagavad Gita and the Yogvashishta into Persian.

s: Which work of Dara Shikoh is a Persian translation of the Upanishads?
x: Sirr-i-Akbar (1657) is Dara's Persian Upanishads; Majma-ul-Bahrain compares Sufism and Vedanta.

s: Because of which of their actions did Shah Jahan defeat the Portuguese at Hughli in 1632?
x: The Portuguese were defeated at Hughli in 1632 over their trading abuses.

s: Who carried away the Peacock Throne, or Takht-i-Taus, from India?
x: Nadir Shah carried away the Peacock Throne from India in 1739. It had stood in the Diwan-i-Khas and was described by Tavernier.

s: In which year was Shah Jahan crowned at Agra?
x: Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in 1628.

s: By what name are the letters on the money dispute between Shah Jahan and his son known?
x: The letters concerning the father-son money dispute between Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb are known as the Adab-i-Alamgiri.

s: Where was Shah Jahan kept under guard after his deposition in 1658?
x: Shah Jahan was confined in Agra Fort and nursed by Jahanara.

s: During whose reign was the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri compiled?
x: The Fatawa-i-Alamgiri belongs to Aurangzeb's reign, not Shah Jahan's 'Golden Age'.

s: In which year did Shah Jahan die as a captive in Agra Fort?
x: Shah Jahan was confined in Agra Fort for about 8 years until his death in 1666.

s: In which field is Shah Jahan's reign called the Mughal 'golden age'?
x: Shah Jahan's reign is the golden age of Mughal architecture (Taj Mahal, Lal Qila, Jama Masjid).

s: Who wrote the Padshahnama of Shah Jahan's reign?
x: Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote the Padshahnama.

s: Which Bundela chief revolted early in Shah Jahan's reign?
x: Shah Jahan's early revolts were by the Bundela Jujhar Singh and Khan Jahan Lodi.

s: Which Mughal emperor abolished sijda (prostration before the emperor)?
x: Sijda, begun by Balban, was ended by Shah Jahan.

s: Which of the following statements about the Mughal emperors is correct?
o: Babur adopted the title Zinda Pir.
Shah Jahan received the title 'Shah Jahan' from Jahangir.
Aurangzeb was known as Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir.
x: Jahangir gave Prince Khurram the title 'Shah Jahan'. Alamgir and Zinda Pir were associated with Aurangzeb, while Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir was Jahangir's title.

s: Which Mughal emperor, slightly more orthodox than Akbar, destroyed some newly built temples yet kept many Hindu nobles?
x: Shah Jahan was slightly more orthodox and destroyed some newly built temples but continued to employ many Hindu nobles.

s: Which traditions does Dara Shikoh's Majma-ul-Bahrain bring together?
x: Majma-ul-Bahrain ('mingling of two oceans') compares Sufism and Vedanta.

s: Of which text is Dara Shikoh's Sirr-i-Akbar (1657) a Persian translation?
x: Sirr-i-Akbar is the Persian Upanishads (1657); the Mahabharata became the Razmnama under Akbar.

s: What is the meaning of the title ‘Shah Jahan’?
x: Shah Jahan means King of the World, a title Prince Khurram took on his accession. Alamgir means Conqueror of the World, Sakari Saka-conqueror and Devanampiya Beloved of the Gods.

s: In which year did Jahangir's eldest son Khusrau rebel?
x: Khusrau rebelled in 1606; Khurram's revolt (1622-26) was the one provoked by Nur Jahan backing Shahryar.

s: Which statement about Mewar during Jahangir's reign is correct?
o: Rana Amar Singh submitted in 1615 and Karan Singh was made a mansabdar.
Karan Singh succeeded Jahangir after Mewar's submission.
Rana Amar Singh defeated Jahangir and ended Mughal control over Mewar.
Rana Amar Singh recovered Kandahar for the Mughals.
x: Amar Singh of Mewar submitted to Jahangir in 1615 and his son Karan Singh was made a mansabdar, ending the long Mughal-Mewar conflict.

s: Whom did Nur Jahan support, which was the immediate political reason for Khurram's revolt?
x: Nur Jahan favoured Shahryar, her son-in-law, as successor. This contributed to Khurram's revolt from 1622 to 1626.

s: With which place is Salim Chishti of Akbar's reign associated?
x: Salim Chishti lived at Sikri in Akbar's time.

s: On the bank of which river did Mahabat Khan seize Jahangir in 1626?
x: Mahabat Khan's coup of 1626 seized Jahangir on the Jhelum.

s: Which of the following did NOT take place in Jahangir's reign?
x: Kabul and Kandahar were not annexed by Jahangir; Kandahar was in fact lost to Persia in 1622.

s: During which years did Prince Khurram revolt against Jahangir?
x: Khurram revolted in 1622-26 when Nur Jahan backed Shahryar as heir.

s: Who was the mother of Prince Khusrau, Jahangir's eldest son?
x: Khusrau's mother was Man Bai; Jagat Gosain was the mother of Shah Jahan.

s: To which Persian ruler did Jahangir lose Kandahar in 1622?
x: Kandahar was lost to Shah Abbas I of Persia in 1622.

s: Who built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah at Agra, noted for its marble inlay and regarded as a precursor of the Taj Mahal?
x: Nur Jahan built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah (her father, Ghiyas Beg) at Agra. Ghiyas Beg was also Jahangir's diwan, and Asaf Khan was his son, but the builder was Nur Jahan; Shah Jahan's father-in-law was Asaf Khan, not Itimad-ud-Daulah.

s: Who was Nur Jahan's father, who served as Jahangir's diwan?
x: Ghiyas Beg was Nur Jahan's father and Jahangir's diwan; Asaf Khan was her brother.

s: Under which pen name did Nur Jahan write poetry?
x: Nur Jahan was also a poet and used the pen name Makhfi.

s: In which year did Nur Jahan marry Jahangir?
x: Nur Jahan married Jahangir in 1611 and received the title Padshah Begum.

s: Which of the following emperor–diwan pairs is correctly matched?
x: Jahangir's diwan was Ghiyas Beg Itimad-ud-Daulah. The other correct pairs are Akbar–Muzaffar Khan, Shah Jahan–Sa'adullah Khan and Aurangzeb–Asad Khan.

s: Which Mughal consort had her name placed on coins and farmans?
x: Nur Jahan was the only Mughal consort whose name appeared on coins and farmans.

s: Whose widow was Mehrunnisa (Nur Jahan) before marrying Jahangir?
x: Mehrunnisa was the widow of Sher Afghan; Asaf Khan was her brother.

s: Which member of Nur Jahan's junta was her brother and Shah Jahan's father-in-law?
x: Asaf Khan was Nur Jahan's brother and father of Mumtaz Mahal; Itimad-ud-Daulah (Ghiyas Beg) was her father.

s: Which title did Nur Jahan later receive?
x: Mehrunnisa was titled Nur Jahan and later Padshah Begum; Sahibat-uz-Zamani was Jahanara's title.

s: In which year did Jahangir lose Kandahar to Persia?
x: Jahangir annexed neither Kabul nor Kandahar; he lost Kandahar to Persia in 1622.

s: Which of the following describes Jahangir's religious policy?
o: A complete break from Akbar's tolerance
Broadly continuing Akbar's tolerance, though Guru Arjan Dev was executed for political reasons
x: Jahangir broadly continued Akbar's tolerance; Guru Arjan Dev was executed for political reasons linked to support for the rebel prince Khusrau.

s: In which monument was Dara Shikoh buried?
x: Dara Shikoh, executed in 1659, was buried in Humayun's Tomb.

s:
Consider the following statements about the battles of the war of succession:
1. Bahadurgarh was fought before Dharmat.
2. Samugarh was fought before Khajwa.
3. Deorai was the first battle of the war.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The order was Bahadurgarh, Dharmat, Samugarh, Khajwa and Deorai (February 1658 to March 1659), so Deorai was the last battle, not the first.

s: Whom did Aurangzeb and Murad decisively defeat at Samugarh (1658)?
x: Samugarh near Agra was the decisive defeat of Dara; Jaswant Singh was beaten at Dharmat and Shuja at Khajwa.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Deorai — final defeat of Dara Shikoh
x: Samugarh was fought near Agra, not near Ajmer. Deorai was near Ajmer, while Khajwa was near Fatehpur and Dharmat was near Ujjain.

s: Who betrayed Dara Shikoh to Aurangzeb?
x: Dara was betrayed by Malik Jiwan of Dadar, executed in 1659 and buried in Humayun's Tomb.

s: Near which place was the Battle of Dharmat (1658) fought?
x: Dharmat was near Ujjain; Samugarh near Agra, Deorai near Ajmer and Bahadurgarh near Banaras.

s: Near which place was the Battle of Deorai (1659), Dara Shikoh's final defeat, fought?
x: Deorai was near Ajmer; Khajwa was near Fatehpur.

s: Where did Shah Shuja flee after his defeat in the war of succession?
x: Shuja fled to Arakan; Murad was imprisoned in Gwalior.

s: In which year was Murad Bakhsh, imprisoned in Gwalior, executed?
x: Murad Bakhsh was imprisoned in Gwalior and executed in 1661.

s: Whom did Aurangzeb and Murad defeat in the Battle of Dharmat (1658)?
x: At Dharmat near Ujjain, Aurangzeb and Murad beat Jaswant Singh, who led Dara's army.

s: Who defeated Shah Shuja at Bahadurgarh near Banaras in 1658?
x: Dara's son Sulaiman Shikoh defeated Shuja at Bahadurgarh in February 1658.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Hawkins — English arrival in India in 1608
Shah Abbas I — recovery of Kandahar in 1638
Guru Arjan Dev — rebellion against Khurram
Mahabat Khan — revolt of Khusrau in 1606
x: Hawkins reached Surat in 1608, in Jahangir's reign. B is wrong because Shah Abbas I captured Kandahar in 1622; its recovery in 1638 was under Shah Jahan, when Ali Mardan Khan surrendered it. C and D are wrong because Guru Arjan Dev backed the rebel Khusrau (not a rebellion against Khurram), and Mahabat Khan's coup was in 1626, not Khusrau's 1606 revolt.

s: In which year was the English factory at Surat established?
x: The Surat factory came in 1613, after Captain Best's 1612 victory over the Portuguese off Surat.

s: What did Sir Thomas Roe's embassy to Jahangir secure for the English?
o: Rights to trade and establish factories
x: Roe obtained rights to trade and set up factories; the title English Khan belonged to William Hawkins.

s: On which ship did William Hawkins reach Surat in 1608?
x: Hawkins came on the Hector to Surat in 1608 and reached Agra in 1609.

s: In whose reign did the first Mughal-British conflict (1686) take place?
x: In 1686 under Aurangzeb, Shaista Khan drove the English out of Hooghly.

s: Which of the following pairs (Visitor – Ruler of the time) is correctly matched?
x: Ibn Battuta came under Muhammad bin Tughluq. Fa-Hien came under Chandragupta II, Hiuen-Tsang under Harsha, and the Portuguese reached Vijayanagara under Krishnadeva Raya.

s: Sir Thomas Roe came to the court of Jahangir as the ambassador of which English king?
x: Sir Thomas Roe was James I's ambassador to Jahangir (1615-19).

s: Where did Jahangir receive Sir Thomas Roe in 1616?
x: Roe was received by Jahangir at Ajmer in 1616 and won trade and factory rights.

s: Which English captain defeated the Portuguese off Surat in 1612, leading to the English factory at Surat?
x: Captain Best beat the Portuguese off Surat in 1612; the Surat factory followed in 1613.

s: Which European traveller described the Peacock Throne of Shah Jahan?
x: The French jeweller Tavernier described the Peacock Throne.

s: Who drove the English under Job Charnock out of Hooghly in 1686?
x: In the first Mughal-British conflict (1686), Shaista Khan drove the English out of Hooghly.

s: In which year did English ships reach Surat?
x: English ships reached Surat in 1608; Hawkins got a firman in 1609 and Roe came in 1615.

s: In which year did Sir Thomas Roe come to the Mughal court?
x: Roe came in 1615; English ships reached Surat in 1608 and Hawkins got a firman in 1609.

s: Shah Jahan recovered Kandahar when its Persian governor surrendered it to the Mughal Empire. Who was that governor?
x: The Persian governor Ali Mardan Khan surrendered Kandahar to Shah Jahan. The recovery is generally dated 1638, though some accounts mention 1639.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: The Balkh-Badakhshan campaign was commanded first by Murad Bakhsh and later by Aurangzeb, not Dara Shikoh. Dara Shikoh commanded the 1653 Kandahar siege.

s: What was the result of the Mughal sieges of Kandahar in 1649, 1652 and 1653?
o: All three failed, and Kandahar was lost permanently.
All three succeeded in recovering Kandahar.
The first two failed but the third established Mughal control.
x: Aurangzeb's sieges in 1649 and 1652 and Dara Shikoh's siege in 1653 all failed; Kandahar was thereafter lost for good.

s: Who led the Mughal siege of Kandahar in 1653, after which it was lost for good?
x: Aurangzeb led the 1649 and 1652 sieges; Dara led the failed 1653 siege.

s: Who led Shah Jahan's Balkh-Badakhshan campaign (1646-47)?
x: The Balkh campaign was led by Murad Bakhsh and then Aurangzeb, not Dara, and failed with heavy losses.

s: Kandahar was recovered by Shah Jahan in 1638. In which year did the Persians capture it again?
x: Kandahar was lost under Jahangir (1622), recovered in 1638 when Ali Mardan Khan surrendered it, and captured by Persia in 1649; the Mughal sieges of 1649, 1652 and 1653 failed, so it was lost for good.

s: Which statement about Abul Hasan Tana Shah is correct?
o: He employed Madanna and Akkanna and helped Shivaji.
He led the Satnami revolt at Narnaul.
He founded the Qutb Shahi dynasty.
x: Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last Qutb Shahi ruler, employed Madanna and Akkanna and helped Shivaji.

s: In which year did the Mughals annex the Nizam Shahi state of Ahmadnagar?
x: Ahmadnagar was annexed under Shah Jahan in 1636; 1687 is the annexation of Golconda.

s: What did the 1636 ahdnamas concluded with Bijapur and Golconda recognise?
x: The agreements recognised Mughal suzerainty, required tribute and provided for Mughal arbitration.

s: Which of the following was one of the four subas into which the Mughal Deccan was reorganised?
x: The four subas were Khandesh, Berar, Telangana and Daulatabad.

s: At whose instigation did Aurangzeb attack Golconda in 1656?
x: Aurangzeb attacked Golconda in 1656 at the instigation of Mir Jumla.

s: Who was Jahangir's envoy to Golconda?
x: Jahangir sent Mir Makki; Mir Jumla is linked with Aurangzeb's 1656 attack on Golconda.

s: Who accepted Golconda's Inqiyad Nama, which placed Shah Jahan's name in the khutba and on coins?
x: Abdullah Qutb Shah's Inqiyad Nama put Shah Jahan's name in the khutba and on coins.

s: During which periods did Aurangzeb serve as viceroy of the Deccan?
x: Aurangzeb was Deccan viceroy in 1636-44 and 1652-58.

s: Which title did Aurangzeb take?
x: Aurangzeb took the title Alamgir; Shah-i-Iqbal was Dara's title.

s: Which Mughal emperor reimposed jizya in 1679?
x: Aurangzeb, called Alamgir and 'Zinda Pir', reimposed jizya in 1679.

s: Under Aurangzeb's jizya, children below what age were exempted?
x: Children below 14 were exempt, along with women, slaves, beggars and the unemployed.

s: Under which Mughal emperor was the share of Hindu nobles in the nobility the highest?
x: Hindu nobles formed about 31.6% under Aurangzeb, against about 22.5% under Akbar.

s:
Consider the following statements about Hindu nobles in Mughal service:
1. Their share under Aurangzeb was higher than under Akbar.
2. Most Hindu nobles added under Aurangzeb were Marathas from the Deccan wars.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Under Aurangzeb Hindu nobles rose to about 31.6%, mostly Marathas taken in during the Deccan wars.

s: Which Mughal emperor banned the celebration of Navroz?
x: Aurangzeb, who also reimposed jizya in 1679, banned Navroz.

s: Which of the following statements about Aurangzeb's coronations is correct?
o: He was crowned once in 1658 before the Battle of Samugarh.
His first hurried coronation took place in 1658 after Samugarh, followed by a grand coronation in 1659 after Deorai.
His first coronation took place in 1659 after Deorai and the second in 1666 at Agra.
He had three coronations, all held at Delhi.
x: Aurangzeb had a hurried first coronation in 1658 after Samugarh and a grand second coronation in 1659 after Deorai.

s: Which title was conferred on Jahanara?
x: Jahanara was honoured as Sahibat-uz-Zamani (Mistress of the Age); Roshanara was made Padshah Begum.

s: What is the name of Aurangzeb's war with the English (1686–90), the first between a Mughal emperor and the English?
x: The Child's War of 1686–90 was the first conflict between the English and a Mughal emperor, fought under Aurangzeb.

s: Aurangzeb was popularly called by which epithet for his simple, pious life?
x: He was popularly known as Zinda Pir ('Living Saint'); Alamgir was his regnal title.

s: Which royal woman received the title Padshah Begum under Aurangzeb?
x: Roshanara, who backed Aurangzeb in the succession war, was Padshah Begum; Jahanara was Sahibat-uz-Zamani.

s: Which regnal title did Aurangzeb assume?
x: Aurangzeb took the regnal title Alamgir, meaning 'World Conqueror'.

s: What happened to newly built temples under Aurangzeb's religious policy?
x: Under Aurangzeb, newly built temples were ordered to be destroyed. His 1669 order led to the demolition of the Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai (Mathura) temples.

s: Which temple was named in Aurangzeb's temple-demolition order of 1669?
x: The 1669 order included Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai at Mathura.

s: What were the officers appointed by Aurangzeb to enforce the Sharia called?
x: Aurangzeb appointed Muhtasibs to enforce the Sharia; he also banned Navroz and discontinued Jharokha darshan.

s: In which year did Aurangzeb reimpose the jizya?
x: Jizya was reimposed in 1679, the year the Rajput war began; 1669 was the temple order.

s:
Consider the following statements about Aurangzeb's religious measures:
1. He stopped jharokha darshan and tuladan.
2. He banned the Navroz celebration.
3. He abolished the jizya.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: He stopped jharokha darshan and tuladan and banned Navroz; he reimposed the jizya, which Akbar had abolished.

s: What were the state-made secular regulations issued under Aurangzeb known as?
x: Zawabit were state-made secular regulations; Aurangzeb stressed the supremacy of Sharia over them.

s: According to Athar Ali, to about what share did Hindu nobles rise under Aurangzeb (1679–1707)?
x: Athar Ali shows the Hindu share in the nobility rose to about 31.6%, many of them Marathas.

s: Which musical instrument did Aurangzeb play, though he banned music at his court?
x: Aurangzeb banned court music, yet he played the veena himself.

s: What does Aurangzeb's title 'Alamgir' mean?
x: Alamgir means 'Conqueror of the World'; Shah Jahan means 'King of the World'.

s: Which tribes were involved in the Afghan revolt against Aurangzeb?
x: The Afghan revolt involved the Yusufzai and Afridi tribes of the north-west.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to revolts against Aurangzeb is correctly matched?
o: Sikhs – Execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur
x: The Sikh resistance is linked with Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution. The Jats were associated with Mathura and Gokula, the Satnamis with Narnaul, and the Rajputs with Marwar, Mewar and Durgadas Rathore.

s: Where was the Satnami revolt against Aurangzeb centred?
x: The Satnamis rose at Narnaul; the Jats at Mathura and Gokula.

s: With whom is the Rajput resistance to Aurangzeb in Marwar associated?
x: Durgadas Rathore led the Rajput resistance in Marwar and Mewar.

s: Around which place was the Jat revolt against Aurangzeb centred?
x: The Jats rose around Mathura and Gokula.

s: In which year did Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar, whose death led to the Rajput war of 1679-81, die?
x: Jaswant Singh died in 1678; Durgadas Rathore then championed his posthumous heir Ajit Singh.

s: What was the result of Aurangzeb's handling of the Marwar and Mewar resistance?
o: The Rajputs becoming the chief pillar of his empire
Peaceful acceptance of the Mughal succession in Marwar
The breaking of the Rajput alliance that had supported Akbar's empire
x: The clumsy handling of Marwar and Mewar broke the Rajput alliance that had been a pillar of Akbar's empire and cost the Mughals considerable influence.

s: Who championed the cause of Ajit Singh, the posthumous son of Jaswant Singh of Marwar?
x: Durgadas Rathore championed Ajit Singh; Rana Raj Singh of Mewar joined Marwar in the war.

s: Who was the rebel Mughal prince who joined the Rajputs in 1681 and later fled to Sambhaji?
x: Aurangzeb's son Prince Akbar joined the Rajputs in 1681, fled to Sambhaji and finally to Persia.

s: Which Mewar ruler joined Marwar in the Rajput war of 1679–81?
x: Rana Raj Singh of Mewar joined Marwar in the war of 1679–81.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Churaman – Jat revolt at Mathura in 1669
Satnami revolt – Foundation of Bharatpur power
Rajaram – Plunder of Akbar's tomb at Sikandra
x: Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb; Gokula led the 1669 Mathura revolt, Churaman founded the power that became Bharatpur, and the Satnamis rose at Narnaul.

s: Where was the Satnami revolt of 1672 centred?
x: The 1672 Satnami revolt of peasants and artisans was centred at Narnaul in Haryana.

s: The Jat power built by Churaman after 1700 became which state?
x: Churaman built the Jat power that became Bharatpur state.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the revolts under Aurangzeb?
o: Gokula led the Jat revolt of 1669 near Mathura.
The Satnami revolt of 1672 was centred at Narnaul.
The Satnami revolt of 1672 was led by Guru Ghasidas.
Jat leader Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra.
x: Guru Ghasidas belongs to the 19th-century Satnampanth of Chhattisgarh and has no link with the Satnami revolt of 1672.

s: Who led the Jat revolt of 1669 in the Mathura region?
x: Gokula led the Jat peasant revolt of 1669 at Tilpat near Mathura against heavy revenue demands.

s: Which Jat leader plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra?
x: In the 1680s the Jat leader Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra; he is different from the Maratha Rajaram.

s: In which year did the Satnami revolt break out at Narnaul?
x: The Satnamis of Narnaul (Haryana) rose in 1672 and were crushed.

s: Maharaja Surajmal, described as 'the Plato of the Jat tribe', ruled which state?
x: Surajmal (ruled 1755-1763) was the Jat ruler of Bharatpur; a contemporary historian called him the Plato of the Jat tribe.

s: In which year was Guru Tegh Bahadur executed by Aurangzeb at Delhi?
x: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the 9th Guru, was executed at Delhi in 1675 after refusing to accept Islam.

s: After which battle did Guru Gobind Singh write the Zafarnama, a Persian letter to Aurangzeb?
x: After Chamkaur (1704) Guru Gobind Singh wrote the Zafarnama accusing Aurangzeb of breaking oaths sworn on the Quran.

s:
Consider the following statements about Sikh resistance to Aurangzeb:
1. Guru Tegh Bahadur was the 9th Sikh Guru.
2. The Zafarnama was written in Punjabi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Guru Tegh Bahadur was the 9th Guru; the Zafarnama was a Persian letter.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the later Maratha resistance to Aurangzeb?
o: Sambhaji – resisted from Jinji; Rajaram – executed in 1689
Sambhaji – released by Bahadur Shah I; Shahu – executed in 1689
Rajaram – released by Bahadur Shah I; Tarabai – surrendered at Jinji
Sambhaji – executed in 1689; Rajaram – resisted from Jinji; Shahu – released by Bahadur Shah I
x: Sambhaji was executed in 1689, Rajaram continued resistance from Jinji, followed by Tarabai, and Shahu was later released by Bahadur Shah I.

s: Where was Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last ruler of Golconda, exiled?
x: Tana Shah was exiled to Daulatabad and died in 1699; Gwalior was where Murad Bakhsh was imprisoned.

s: Which Maratha queen is associated with the resistance against Aurangzeb?
x: Shivaji, Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai are all associated with the Maratha resistance against Aurangzeb.

s: Who was the last ruler of Bijapur when Aurangzeb annexed it in 1686?
x: Sikandar Adil Shah was the last ruler of Bijapur; Tana Shah was Golconda's.

s: In which year did Aurangzeb annex Golconda?
x: Golconda was annexed in 1687 as the 21st suba; Bijapur fell in 1686.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Abdullah Pani — Defender of Golconda honoured by Aurangzeb
Abul Hasan Qutb Shah — Imprisoned at Bidar and Daulatabad
Abdur Razzaq Lari — Honoured as Mustafa Khan
Tana Shah — Died in 1699 and buried at Khuldabad
x: Abdullah Pani was the traitor who opened the gates of Golconda. Abdur Razzaq Lari was the defender who was honoured as Mustafa Khan.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Mughal conquest of Golconda?
o: Madanna and Akkanna were murdered in 1686.
Its last ruler, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, was exiled to Gwalior.
x: Tana Shah was exiled to Daulatabad, not Gwalior (where Murad Bakhsh was imprisoned).

s: The fall of Golconda to Aurangzeb in 1687 ended the rule of which dynasty over Andhra?
x: Golconda fell in 1687 and Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah) was imprisoned, ending Qutb Shahi rule over Andhra; Golconda became a Mughal suba.

s: Who was the last Adil Shahi ruler of Bijapur, defeated by Aurangzeb in 1686?
x: Sikandar Adil Shah was presented in silver chains and sent to Daulatabad when Bijapur fell in 1686.

s: Which traitor opened the gates of Golconda fort to the Mughals in 1687?
x: Abdullah Pani opened the gates; Abdur Razzaq Lari was the loyal defender.

s: Bhakta Ramadasu was the nephew of which Golconda ministers?
x: Bhakta Ramadasu was the nephew of Akkanna–Madanna, the ministers murdered in 1686.

s: Where was Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah) finally kept after the fall of Golconda?
x: Tana Shah was imprisoned at Bidar, then Daulatabad; Gwalior was where Murad Bakhsh was held.

s: Which event is associated with Shivaji's visit to Agra in 1666?
o: He was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad.
He began the campaign from Jinji.
He was insulted, placed under house arrest and escaped in fruit baskets.
He captured Sirhind from Wazir Khan.
x: During his 1666 visit to Agra, Shivaji was insulted and placed under house arrest, from which he escaped in fruit baskets.

s: Why was the prolonged 27-year Deccan war described as the 'Deccan Ulcer'?
o: prevented the annexation of Bijapur and Golconda
drained the Mughal treasury through prolonged warfare
strengthened the Mughal treasury through continuous tribute
x: The 27-year Deccan war drained the Mughal treasury and was therefore called the 'Deccan Ulcer', in comparison with Napoleon's Spanish Ulcer.

s: Where was Sambhaji captured before his execution in 1689?
x: Sambhaji was captured at Sangameshwar and executed in March 1689.

s: Who led the Maratha war against Aurangzeb from 1700 as regent for her infant son Shivaji II?
x: Tarabai, Rajaram's widow, led the war from 1700 as regent for Shivaji II.

s: From which fort did Rajaram resist the Mughals after becoming Chhatrapati in 1689?
x: Rajaram resisted from Jinji and died at Sinhagad in 1700.

s: Where did the Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram die in 1700?
x: Rajaram, who resisted from Jinji, died at Sinhagad in 1700.

s: Where was Aurangzeb, who died at Ahmednagar in 1707, buried?
x: He was buried in a simple grave at Khuldabad near Aurangabad, where Tana Shah was also buried.

s: Where did Aurangzeb die in 1707?
x: Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in 1707 and was buried at Khuldabad.

s: Which last Golconda ruler is also buried at Khuldabad, the burial place of Aurangzeb?
x: Tana Shah (Abul Hasan Qutb Shah) died in 1699 and was buried at Khuldabad, where Aurangzeb also lies.

s: Under which emperor did the Mughal Empire reach its maximum territorial extent?
x: Aurangzeb's Deccan conquests of Bijapur and Golconda gave the empire its greatest extent.

s: In which year did Aurangzeb annex Golconda as the 21st Mughal suba?
x: Aurangzeb annexed Golconda on 3 October 1687; 1679 is the year jizya was revived.

s: What did a mansab denote under Akbar's Mansabdari system?
x: A mansab was a rank serving military and civil administration, not a hereditary office.

s: What normally happened to ranks and jagirs under the Mansabdari system?
o: Ended with the death of the holder
Passed to the holder's eldest son
x: Mansabs were not hereditary; ranks and jagirs normally ended with the holder's death.

s: What was payment to a mansabdar in cash known as?
x: Mansabdars were paid in cash (naqd) or by non-hereditary assignment of land revenue (jagir).

s: What kind of rank was the mansab, on which the Mughal central administration rested?
x: Every officer held a mansab, a combined military-cum-civil rank, which is why the Mughal state was essentially military.

s: What was the range of mansab ranks under the Mansabdari system?
x: Ranks ran from 10 to 10,000, the highest reserved for princes.

s: According to Abul Fazl, how many mansab grades existed in theory?
x: Abul Fazl gives 66 grades in theory, of which 33 existed in practice.

s: Who introduced the Mansabdari system in Mughal India?
x: Akbar introduced the mansabdari system, giving every army and civil officer a rank (mansab).

s: From where was the model of the Mughal mansabdari system borrowed?
o: Central Asia (Mongol decimal grading of the army)
x: The mansabdari model came from Central Asia, from the decimal army grading of Genghis Khan's Mongols.

s: What did 'sawar' denote in the Mughal Mansabdari system?
x: Sawar indicated the number of cavalrymen to be maintained; zat was personal rank and status.

s: Which of the following pairs regarding classes of mansabdars is correctly matched?
o: First class – Sawar less than half of zat
First class – Sawar half of zat
Third class – Sawar equal to zat
Second class – Sawar half of zat
x: Second-class mansabdars had sawar equal to half of zat. First class had sawar equal to zat and third class had sawar less than half of zat.

s: With the reign of which Mughal emperor was the conditional increase in sawar rank known as mashrut associated?
x: Aurangzeb introduced mashrut, a temporary increase in the sawar rank connected with a specific assignment.

s: Under Shah Jahan, what was a jagir yielding half its assessed revenue called?
x: A half-yield jagir was shashmaha and a quarter-yield jagir sihmaha.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the du-aspa sih-aspa arrangement?
o: It raised the zat rank of the mansabdar.
Part of the sawar rank was counted double.
x: Du-aspa sih-aspa counted part of the sawar rank twice for trusted mansabdars without raising their zat.

s: Under Shah Jahan's month-scale, how much did a 'sihmaha' jagir yield?
o: A quarter of its assessed revenue
x: Sihmaha meant a quarter-yield; shashmaha meant half-yield.

s:
Consider the following statements about zat and sawar:
1. Zat denoted personal rank, status and salary.
2. The sawar rank could exceed the zat rank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Zat was the personal rank; under the system the sawar could not exceed the zat.

s: Which Mughal emperor introduced the du-aspa sih-aspa system?
x: Jahangir introduced du-aspa sih-aspa, under which part of a mansabdar's sawar rank was counted double without raising his zat.

s: Under the mansabdari system, how many horses had to be kept for every 10 sawars?
x: The horse rule required 20 horses for every 10 sawars (cavalrymen).

s: What were gentlemen troopers recruited and paid directly by the Mughal emperor called?
x: Ahadis were recruited directly by the emperor; Tabinan were mansabdars' contingents, dakhili state-paid troops under mansabdars, Walashahi the bodyguard.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Mughal army is NOT correct?
o: The entire army consisted exclusively of ahadis recruited directly by the emperor.
The bulk of the army consisted of the cavalry contingents of mansabdars.
Artillery and infantry supplemented the cavalry arm.
Mansabdars’ contingents could be paid through cash or jagir assignments.
x: The Mughal army was not composed exclusively of ahadis. Its bulk consisted of mansabdars’ cavalry contingents, supplemented by infantry and artillery, with different categories of state and personal troops.

s: What were state-paid troops placed under mansabdars in the Mughal army called?
x: Dakhili were state-paid troops under mansabdars; tabinan were the mansabdars' own contingents.

s: What were the mansabdars' own contingents in the Mughal army known as?
x: Tabinan were the mansabdars' own contingents; ahadis were the emperor's own troopers.

s: What did 'dagh' refer to in Mughal military administration?
x: Dagh was horse branding; chehra was the descriptive roll and tashiha the muster check.

s: What did the Mughal term 'tashiha' mean?
x: Tashiha was the muster check, alongside dagh (branding) and chehra (descriptive roll).

s:
Consider the following statements about Mughal muster terms:
1. Chehra was the descriptive roll of soldiers.
2. Akbar revived the dagh and chehra.
3. Walashahi was the emperor's bodyguard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: chehra was the descriptive roll, Akbar revived dagh and chehra, and walashahi was the bodyguard.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Mughal central ministers?
o: Wazir or Diwan – finance and revenue
Mir Bakhshi – military pay, mansabs and intelligence
Mir Saman – religion, charity and madad-i-maash grants
Sadr-us-Sudur – religion, charity and madad-i-maash grants
x: The Mir Saman supervised the royal household and karkhanas; religion and charity were under the Sadr-us-Sudur.

s: What did the authority of the Wakil largely become under Akbar?
x: Although the Wakil had traditionally been the chief adviser or regent, the office became largely symbolic under Akbar.

s: Under which official did Mughal intelligence, run through waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras, come?
x: Intelligence was under the Mir Bakhshi.

s: Which Mughal central official supervised the royal household and the karkhanas?
x: The Mir Saman supervised the royal household and karkhanas.

s: Who was the Mughal chief justice who administered the Sharia?
x: The Qazi-ul-Quzat was the chief justice under the Sharia.

s: Who were the 'waqia-navis' in the Mughal espionage system?
x: Waqia-navis were news-writers; khufia-navis wrote secret reports and harkaras were runners/spies.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Tashiha — verification and muster of troops and horses
Chehra — descriptive roll of a trooper
Dagh — preparation of revenue papers by the assistant to the amalguzar
x: Dagh was the branding of horses to prevent substitution. Preparation of revenue papers and accounts was the duty of the Bitikchi.

s: Which of the following contributed to the decline of the Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb?
o: Loss of Bengal to the Marathas
x: The jagir crisis, along with the Deccan wars and Rajput alienation, contributed to the decline.

s: What were madad-i-maash grants generally?
o: Transferable assignments made to cavalrymen in lieu of salary
Crown lands reserved for the imperial treasury
Revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men under the Sadr
x: Madad-i-maash consisted of revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men and was administered under the Sadr.

s: What was a perpetual Mughal jagir grant called?
x: Altamgha was perpetual; Tankhwah was in lieu of salary, Watan hereditary in the homeland and Mashrut conditional.

s: What was a Watan jagir?
o: The hereditary home territory of a zamindar or Rajput chief
A grant in lieu of salary
A grant subject to conditions of service
x: Watan jagirs were hereditary home territories and were not transferred by the state.

s: Which of the following was NOT a jagir in the Mughal system?
x: Khalisa was crown land, not a jagir; tankhwah, watan and in'am were jagir types.

s: What was a Mughal jagir granted free of any service obligation called?
x: In'am was free of service; tankhwah was in lieu of salary and mashrut was conditional.

s: Why were Mughal jagirs frequently transferred, generally after about three to four years?
o: To convert all jagirs into Khalisa lands
To make them hereditary among local chiefs
To prevent mansabdars from developing local roots and becoming independent feudal lords
To ensure that peasants elected their revenue collectors
x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.

s: What does the term 'bejagiri' refer to?
o: Mansabdars were kept waiting without jagirs
Mansabdars were appointed as village accountants
Revenue was transferred directly to the imperial treasury
Jagirs became hereditary in the home territories of chiefs
x: Bejagiri meant that mansabdars remained without jagir assignments. It bred discontent and factionalism at the imperial court.

s: Which of the following explains the jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb?
o: Reduction of nobility through the exclusion of Deccani and Maratha nobles
Growth in mansabdars, shrinkage of good jagirs and increasing pressure on peasants
Decline in mansabdars, expansion of profitable land and relief to peasants
Abolition of jagirs and complete transfer of revenue collection to village panchayats
x: Under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars increased, profitable jagirs became scarce, and peasants were subjected to intensified extraction.

s: The breakdown of which system is regarded as a core explanation of the decline of the Mughal Empire?
x: The breakdown of the jagirdari system, known as the jagirdari crisis, is a core explanation of Mughal decline.

s: Which historian explained the Mughal jagirdari crisis as a shortage of jagirs relative to claimants?
x: Satish Chandra stressed the shortage of jagirs; Irfan Habib the agrarian crisis; Athar Ali the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles.

s: Which of the following states retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration?
o: Qutb Shahi state of Golconda only
x: The Asaf Jahi state of Hyderabad retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration.

s: Which historian explained the jagirdari crisis as an agrarian crisis?
x: Irfan Habib saw it as an agrarian crisis; Satish Chandra stressed a shortage of jagirs.

s: To what did Athar Ali mainly link the jagirdari crisis?
o: The influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles
x: Athar Ali stressed the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles under Aurangzeb.

s: Under Aurangzeb, what was the pool of land held back for assignment as jagirs, which proved too small for the growing number of mansabdars, called?
x: Paibaqi was land kept unassigned, available for allotment as jagirs; under Aurangzeb more mansabdars and too little good paibaqi land squeezed the peasants. Khalisa was crown land, Altamgha a hereditary grant and Watan a hereditary home jagir.

s: How many subahs were there by the end of Akbar's reign?
x: Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580 and 15 by the end of his reign; Aurangzeb had 21.

s: Above which unit did the pargana stand immediately in the Mughal administrative hierarchy?
x: The order from lowest to highest was village, pargana, sarkar and subah, so the pargana stood just above the village.

s: Which of the following is the correct ascending order of Mughal administrative units?
x: From smallest to largest the units were village, pargana, sarkar and subah (province).

s: Besides the Faujdar, who was the principal official of a Mughal Sarkar?
x: A Sarkar was run by the Faujdar and Amalguzar; a Suba by the Subedar and provincial Diwan.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Chakla is correct?
o: It was a unit between the Suba and Pargana and was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
It was a military rank assigned to a Mansabdar.
It was identical with the Sarkar in every province.
It was the smallest village-level revenue unit.
x: Chakla was a unit between the Suba and Pargana, but it was not identical with the Sarkar. It was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.

s: At which level did the effective reach of Mughal rural administration generally end?
x: The state's effective reach ended at the Pargana; villages were largely self-governing.

s: How many subas did the Mughal empire have under Aurangzeb?
x: Akbar began with 12 and had 15 by the end of his reign; Aurangzeb had 21, Golconda being the 21st.

s: Under whom was the Chakla, a unit not identical with the sarkar, prominent in Bengal?
x: The chakla was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.

s: Who formalised the Dahsala settlement of 1580?
x: Raja Todar Mal formalised the zabt system as the Dahsala settlement in 1580.

s: Under the Dahsala system, revenue was fixed on the average yield of how many past years?
x: Dahsala rates were based on the average yield of the past ten years, payable in cash.

s: In which regions was Nasaq, an estimate based on past assessments, mainly used?
x: Nasaq was used in Bengal and Orissa.

s: Which Mughal revenue system was based on sharing of the crop?
x: Batai (ghallabakhshi or bhaoli) shared the crop; kankut estimated the crop.

s: Which Mughal revenue system was based on an estimate of the crop?
x: Kankut fixed revenue by estimating the standing crop; batai was crop-sharing.

s: In Akbar's land classification, what was land cultivated every year called?
x: Polaj land was cultivated every year; parauti was left fallow for a short time.

s: How was land left uncultivated for five years or more classed?
x: Banjar land lay uncultivated 5 years or more; chachar lay fallow 3–4 years.

s: In a Mughal province, which official managed revenue and acted as an independent check on the governor?
x: The provincial Diwan managed revenue and checked the Subahdar, who handled governance and law and order.

s: Who kept land records and revenue papers in a Mughal sarkar?
x: The Bitikchi kept land records and revenue papers; the Khazanadar was the treasurer.

s: Who was the head of the patwaris at the pargana level?
x: The Qanungo headed the patwaris and kept records; the Karkun was a clerk.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Kotwal handled town police and markets; the Shiqdar was the pargana executive and the Khazanadar the treasurer.

s: Who was in charge of military command and law and order in a Mughal sarkar?
x: The faujdar headed the sarkar's military and kept law and order; the kotwal policed towns.

s: Who was the executive and police officer at the pargana level in Mughal administration?
x: The Shiqdar headed the executive and police work of a pargana; the Faujdar worked at the sarkar level.

s: Who was the village accountant in Mughal administration?
x: The Patwari was the village accountant; the Qanungo was head of the patwaris at pargana level.

s: Why was the provincial Diwan in the Mughal administration independent of the Subedar?
o: controlled the city police and markets
served as a check on the Subedar in revenue and finance
x: The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.

s: Which Mughal city official was in charge of police, markets and a watch on newcomers?
x: The Kotwal was the city police chief who also controlled markets and watched newcomers.

s: In Mughal provincial administration, what did the Diwan-i-Tan deal with?
x: The Diwan-i-Tan handled salaries (tankhwah) and jagir assignments.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Muhtasib looked after public morals; the Bakhshi handled military pay and musters.

s: By which other name was the Subedar, the governor of a Mughal suba, known?
x: The Subedar, governor of a suba, was also called Nazim or Sipahsalar.

s: Which of the following pairs (Official – Duty) is correctly matched?
x: The Potdar was the treasurer. The Bitikchi prepared assessment and land records, the Qanungo kept pargana-level records and the Patwari was the village accountant.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Muqaddam — Village headman and revenue collector
Khazanadar — Keeper of hereditary land records
x: The Muqaddam, or Patel, was the village headman and collected revenue. The Khazanadar or Fotadar was the treasurer at the Sarkar level.

s: In a Mughal sarkar, what was the role of the Potdar or Khazanadar?
x: The Potdar (Khazanadar/Fotadar) was the sarkar treasurer; the Bitikchi was the accountant.

s: Who was the official responsible for collecting revenue in charge of a district?
x: The amalguzar, also called amil, was the district-level revenue collector.

s: Who was the Mughal village headman who also collected revenue?
x: The Muqaddam (Patel) was the village headman; the Patwari was the village accountant.

s: In the Mughal system, in lieu of what was a jagir given to a mansabdar?
o: judicial and police duties in the area
x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary and military service; they carried no judicial or police duties (UPSC 2019 key: a statement linking jagirs to judicial/police duties is wrong). A jagir gave no ownership of land, and revenue-free grants for scholars and holy men were madad-i-maash.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a jagirdar from a zamindar?
o: A jagirdar held hereditary local rights, whereas a zamindar was frequently transferred
A jagirdar held a revenue assignment in lieu of salary, whereas a zamindar possessed hereditary local rights and acted as an intermediary
A zamindar was appointed only as a provincial governor, whereas a jagirdar was a village accountant
Both were hereditary proprietors of land with identical powers
x: A mansabdar holding a jagir had a non-hereditary right to collect revenue in lieu of salary and was frequently transferred. A zamindar held hereditary rights over land revenue and local power and acted as an intermediary between the state and peasants.

s: In which sequence was a Mansabdar paid through a tankhwah jagir connected to revenue collection?
o: Mansabdar — Tankhwah jagir — Jagirdar's agents — Zamindars — Peasant
x: The Mansabdar got a rank and was paid by a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected the assessed revenue (jama) through the zamindars, who kept a hereditary share, and the peasant paid about one-third of the produce.

s: In the Mughal revenue system, the peasant generally paid approximately what share of the produce?
x: The peasant's payment was approximately one-third of the produce in the mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar revenue linkage.

s: Which of the following was a major local manifestation of the jagirdari crisis?
o: Zamindars became salaried imperial officials and peasants received remissions permanently.
The state abolished revenue collection through local intermediaries.
Short-tenure Jagirdars pressed for more revenue, zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants fled.
Jagirdars reduced demands and zamindars abandoned cultivation.
x: Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.

s: In lieu of what were Mughal jagirs given as revenue assignments?
o: Salary for state, mainly military, service
x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary for state service; they were not hereditary and were often transferred.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about jagirdars and zamindars?
o: Jagirdars received revenue in lieu of salary.
Jagirdars held hereditary rights over land.
x: Jagirdars' rights were not hereditary; zamindars held hereditary, saleable rights.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the categories of zamindars in Mughal India?
o: Autonomous chiefs were Rajas ruling their own territories.
Primary zamindars held only temporary, non-hereditary rights over land.
Intermediary zamindars collected revenue from primary zamindars for a commission.
Autonomous chiefs paid tribute and served as mansabdars.
x: Primary zamindars did not hold merely temporary, non-hereditary rights; the other three statements are correct.

s: Which historian classified Mughal zamindars as autonomous chiefs, intermediary and primary?
x: The three categories of zamindars are S. Nurul Hasan's classification.

s: What were Mughal zamindars who collected revenue from primary zamindars for the state in return for a commission called?
x: Intermediary zamindars collected from primary zamindars for the state and got a commission.

s: Under Tana Shah, Qutb Shahi Golconda was divided into how many Sarkars?
x: Golconda was organised into tarafs and simalu, with 37 Sarkars and 517 Parganas under Tana Shah.

s: How was land revenue mainly handled in Qutb Shahi Golconda?
o: Assessed only through the Dahsala system
Collected by village panchayats without intermediaries
Assessed only through Kankut crop estimates
x: Qutb Shahi Golconda farmed out its revenue by auction; the Northern Circars zamindars date from that era.

s: What was the village accountant called in Qutb Shahi Golconda?
x: The kulkarni was the accountant; the mukaddam was the village head and the desai the pargana officer.

s: Under Tana Shah, Qutb Shahi Golconda had how many parganas?
x: Under Tana Shah Golconda had 37 sarkars and 517 parganas.

s: What were the provincial units of Qutb Shahi Golconda called?
x: Qutb Shahi Golconda was divided into tarafs and simalu.

s: The zamindaris of which Andhra region date from the Qutb Shahi era?
x: The zamindars of the Northern Circars date from the Qutb Shahi period.

s: Which French physician was linked with Dara Shikoh and later attended Aurangzeb's court?
x: Bernier, a French physician, was linked with Dara and later Aurangzeb; Manucci was a Venetian.

s: Who is the author of 'Storia do Mogor'?
x: The Venetian Niccolao Manucci, Dara's artilleryman, wrote Storia do Mogor.

s: Which traveller, around 1690, traced the route of silver into India?
x: Careri (c. 1690) traced the route by which silver reached India.

s: Who was the French traveller and physician who reached Surat in 1666?
x: Thevenot reached Surat in 1666; Manucci was Italian, Pelsaert Dutch and Mundy English.

s: Which European traveller held that there was no private property in land in Mughal India?
x: Bernier held that private property in land did not exist, a view modern historians have contested.

s: Francois Bernier, who visited the Mughal Empire during 1656–1668, was associated with which of the following positions and patrons?
o: Physician of Shah Jahan and patronised by Mir Jumla
Physician of Dara Shikoh and patronised by Danishmand Khan
Physician of Aurangzeb and patronised by Shaista Khan
Physician of Jahangir and patronised by Asaf Khan
x: Francois Bernier was a French doctor who served as physician to Dara Shikoh and received the patronage of Danishmand Khan.

s: Which of the following were among Bernier's observations on the Mughal economy?
o: Private ownership of all land, agrarian prosperity and outflow of precious metals
Imperial ownership of land, agrarian ruin, inflow of precious metals and prosperity of merchants
Village ownership of land, decline of trade and absence of merchants
Merchant ownership of land, peasant prosperity and exclusive use of copper currency
x: Bernier believed that the emperor owned all land and blamed this arrangement for agrarian ruin. He nevertheless acknowledged that precious metals flowed into India and that merchants prospered.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Fall of the Mughal Empire — M. Athar Ali
Early Travels in India, 1583-1619 — William Foster
Travels in the Mogul Empire, 1656-1668 — Francois Bernier
The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707 — Irfan Habib
x: *Fall of the Mughal Empire* was written by Jadunath Sarkar. M. Athar Ali wrote *The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb*.

s: Which European traveller described the famine during Shah Jahan's reign?
x: Peter Mundy described the famine in Shah Jahan's reign. Pelsaert wrote Remonstrantie, Manucci Storia do Mogor and Tavernier Six Voyages.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Tapan Raychaudhuri — Co-editor of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I
Tavernier — The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707
x: Tapan Raychaudhuri was a co-editor, along with Irfan Habib, of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I. Six Voyages was associated with Tavernier, Early Travels in India with William Foster, and Storia do Mogor with Niccolao Manucci.

s: What was William Foster's role in 'Early Travels in India, 1583–1619'?
x: Foster was the editor, not the author, of Early Travels in India, 1583–1619.

s: Who wrote 'The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb'?
x: M. Athar Ali wrote The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb; Jadunath Sarkar wrote Fall of the Mughal Empire.

s: According to Tavernier, where did the Koh-i-Noor come from?
x: Tavernier recorded that the Koh-i-Noor came from Kollur.

s: Who was J.B. Tavernier in the context of Mughal-period India?
o: Dutch VOC merchant who spent seven years in Agra
English merchant who recorded a famine during Shah Jahan's reign
French diamond merchant who visited the diamond mines of Golconda
French physician who served Dara Shikoh
x: Tavernier was a French gem and diamond merchant who made six visits to India and described the diamond mines of Golconda. The other descriptions relate to Bernier, Pelsaert and Peter Mundy.

s: Who wrote *India at the Death of Akbar*?
x: *India at the Death of Akbar* was written by W. H. Moreland.

s: During whose reign did Francisco Pelsaert arrive in India in 1620?
x: Pelsaert came in Jahangir's time, in 1620.

s: Who was a co-editor of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Vol. I, with Irfan Habib?
x: Tapan Raychaudhuri and Irfan Habib co-edited Vol. I of the Cambridge Economic History of India.

s: Niccolao Manucci, author of Storia do Mogor, was a traveller from which country?
x: Manucci was a Venetian (Italian) who served as an artilleryman and later as a physician in Mughal India.

s: Francisco Pelsaert, who came to India in 1620, was a traveller from which country?
x: Pelsaert was a Dutch factor who came in Jahangir's reign and wrote the Remonstrantie.

s: Who is the author of 'Storia do Mogor'?
x: Storia do Mogor was written by the Venetian Niccolao Manucci.

s: Which traveller wrote the 'Remonstrantie' on the reign of Jahangir?
x: The Dutch factor Francisco Pelsaert, who came in 1620, wrote the Remonstrantie.

s: Which traveller wrote 'Six Voyages'?
x: The French diamond merchant Tavernier, who made six visits to India, wrote Six Voyages.

s: Who is the author of 'Fall of the Mughal Empire'?
x: Fall of the Mughal Empire was written by Jadunath Sarkar.

s: In the Mughal period, what were money-changers and bankers who issued hundis called?
x: Sarrafs were money-changers and bankers issuing hundis; Mahajans were moneylenders-cum-merchants and Baniks retail traders.

s: To which merchant community did the Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals belong?
x: The Marwaris comprised Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals; Chettis were Coromandel merchants.

s: Who was the head of a merchant community and dealt with government officials?
x: The nagarseth was the head of a merchant community and acted as its representative in dealings with officials.

s: In the Sultanate period, before the Mughal pattern of trade took shape, overseas trade was largely in the hands of which merchants?
x: Under the Sultanate, overseas trade was dominated by Multanis and Khurasanis. Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants handled inland trade, so option D is wrong. Chettis were later Coromandel merchants and Marwaris a Rajasthan inland group (B); Banjaras carried bulk goods overland and Baniks were local traders (C).

s: Which Mughal-period traders were mainly local retail traders?
x: Baniks or Beoparis were local retail traders; Seths and Bohras carried on wholesale long-distance trade.

s: In the Mughal period, in which trade were Seths and Bohras mainly engaged?
x: Seths and Bohras were wholesale, long-distance traders; Baniks were local retail traders.

s: Who were the Mahajans of the Mughal period?
o: Bulk carriers of grain and salt
x: Mahajans were moneylenders-cum-merchants.

s: The Chettis of the Mughal period were merchants of which coast?
x: The Chettis were Coromandel coast merchants; Muslim merchants dominated Malabar trade.

s: In the Mughal period, who dominated trade on the Malabar coast?
x: Muslim merchants dominated Malabar trade, while Chettis were Coromandel merchants.

s: For what were the Banjaras primarily known?
x: Banjaras transported grain in bullock caravans and played an important role in internal supply networks.

s: What was bima in the Mughal commercial system?
o: Insurance of goods in transit against a premium
A cash receipt issued by a banik
A royal order issued by the emperor
A land deed issued under the Zabt system
x: Bima was insurance for goods in transit, underwritten by sarrafs for a premium.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the shroffs of Mughal India?
o: They kept deposits and lent money.
x: A farman was a royal order, not a shroff's instrument; shroffs tested coins, kept deposits, lent money and issued hundis.

s: Where was the first European trade centre in Andhra established in the early modern period?
x: Machilipatnam was the first European trade centre in Andhra, established by the Dutch in 1605. Guntur was associated with the Tobacco Board, while Nizampatnam (Petapoli) received European factories only later.

s: Masulipatnam, the Qutb Shahi port, was noted for which textile?
x: Masulipatnam was a Qutb Shahi (Golconda) port noted for Kalamkari, also called chintz, textiles.

s: Which of the following ports was a Portuguese base in Bengal until Shah Jahan expelled the Portuguese in 1632?
x: Hugli was the Portuguese settlement and base in Bengal; Shah Jahan expelled them in 1632.

s:
Consider the following statements about European trade at Masulipatnam:
1. The Dutch set up their factory at Masulipatnam before the English.
2. The French arrived at Masulipatnam before Shah Jahan expelled the Portuguese from Hugli.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Dutch came to Masulipatnam in 1605 and the English in 1611. The French arrived only in 1669, after the Portuguese were expelled from Hugli in 1632.

s: Which of the following centres was associated with saltpetre in the early modern Andhra region?
x: Saltpetre was associated with Machilipatnam, Narsapur and Pulicat. Nirmal was known for Damascus swords and Warangal for carpets or durries.

s: Lahari Bandar, a major 17th-century port, served which city?
x: Lahari Bandar was the port of Thatta in the Indus delta (Sind).

s: Which old Gujarat port declined because of silting?
x: Cambay (Khambhat) was an old Gujarat port that declined with silting.

s: Where was copper traded in the early modern Andhra region?
x: Copper was traded at Motupalli.

s: Which Mughal port was known as Bab-ul-Makka (Gate of Mecca)?
x: Surat, the chief west-coast port, was called Bab-ul-Makka because Haj pilgrims sailed from it.

s: Which centre in the Andhra-Telangana region was famous for Damascus swords?
x: Nirmal was known for Damascus swords.

s: Which centre was famous for carpets and durries in the Qutb Shahi period?
x: Warangal was noted for carpets and durries.

s: Where is the Tobacco Board of India located?
x: The Tobacco Board is at Guntur; Andhra Pradesh is a top tobacco producer.

s: How many dams were equivalent to one rupee in the Mughal monetary system?
x: Forty copper dams were equivalent to one rupee. The dam was the copper denomination, while the rupiya was the silver coin.

s: The silver rupiya that continued under Akbar had been standardised earlier by which ruler, and at what weight?
x: Sher Shah fixed the silver rupiya at 178 grains, and Akbar continued it. Forty copper dams made one rupee.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Chalni — Coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount
x: Chalni referred to coins of the current reign in circulation. Coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount were called Khazana.

s: What did the term 'Sikka' denote in the Mughal monetary system?
o: the copper coin equal to one-fortieth of a rupee
the gold coin used for long-distance trade
coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount
the right of coinage in the ruler's name, signifying sovereignty along with the khutba
x: Sikka denoted the right of coinage in the ruler's name and, together with the khutba, symbolised sovereignty. The other options describe the dam, khazana and mohur respectively.

s: In the Mughal monetary system, what were 'chalni' coins?
o: Newly minted in the current year
In circulation in the current reign
x: Chalni coins were in circulation in the current reign; khazana coins were minted in earlier reigns.

s: What was the Mughal gold coin called?
x: Mohur was gold, rupiya silver and dam copper.

s: According to Thevenot, coins of which metal alone were minted at Golconda?
x: Golconda minted only copper; Mughal silver circulated there.

s:
Consider the following statements about Mughal land classes:
1. Chachar land lay fallow for 3–4 years.
2. Parauti paid the polaj rate when cultivated.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: chachar lay fallow 3–4 years, and parauti paid the polaj rate when cultivated.

s: What did the Mughal term 'jins-i-kamil', meaning 'perfect crops', refer to?
o: Crops reserved exclusively for royal kitchens
x: Jins-i-kamil referred to commercial or superior cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, indigo, oilseeds and opium.

s: Which of the following sets consists of crops that came to India through the Portuguese from the New World?
x: Tobacco and maize (and also chillies) came from the New World via the Portuguese. Pepper, spices, oilseeds, cotton, indigo, opium, rice, wheat and sugarcane were established Indian crops.

s: Bengal in the Mughal period was noted for which crops?
x: Bengal was noted for sugar and rice; Gujarat for indigo and food grains.

s: The Shahab Nahr was built by restoring which earlier canal?
x: The Shahab Nahr was constructed by restoring the Rajabwah canal of Firuz Shah.

s: About what share of rural produce reached the market in the Mughal period?
x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (About 15%); it is added as option 5.
Old app notes: 25% (said to be the APPSC G2 2017 key). PYQ bank key: 15%. No library or web source found to settle it.
The printed key of the APPSC G2 2017 PYQ (two copies) on this fact is about 15%, not 25%; cash revenue pushed peasants to sell part of the crop. The 25% in the old notes is not backed by a source in the library.

s: Which of the following kingdoms is credited with developing agriculture by building ponds, tanks, dams and wells?
x: The Vijayanagara rulers developed agriculture through ponds, tanks, dams and wells.

s: Under the Zabt system, at what was the state share fixed?
o: One-half of the produce of the current year
One-third of the average produce of the past ten years
One-fourth of the average produce of the preceding five years
One-sixth of the average produce of the preceding twelve years
x: The state share was one-third of the average produce calculated over the past ten years.

s:
Consider the following statements about land categories under Akbar's revenue system:
1. Polaj was land cultivated annually.
2. Chachar was land left fallow for three to four years.
3. Banjar was land left fallow for one year.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Polaj was cultivated annually and Chachar lay fallow for three to four years. Banjar was uncultivated land; land fallow for one year was Parauti.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Patta – deed of agreement; Qabuliyat – title deed
Patta – surveyor's fee; Qabuliyat – collector's fee
Patta – title deed; Qabuliyat – deed of agreement
Patta – royal order; Qabuliyat – cash receipt
x: The Patta was the title deed and the Qabuliyat the deed of agreement in the revenue arrangement.

s: Who was the architect of Akbar's Zabt (Bandobast) system, and which instrument was used to measure land?
o: Sher Shah — bamboo rod without iron rings
x: The Zabt system was devised by Akbar's revenue minister Raja Todarmal, and land was measured with the Ilahi Gaz, a bamboo rod joined with iron rings. Option B pairs Todarmal with the wrong gaz; option C names the Mir Saman, who supervised karkhanas; option D names the wrong author and the wrong rod.

s: What was one important economic consequence of collecting land revenue in cash under the zabt system?
o: It monetised the rural economy and linked peasants to markets.
It replaced agricultural production with pastoral activity.
It abolished all forms of rural credit.
It weakened the connection between peasants and markets.
x: Cash revenue under zabt monetised the rural economy and connected peasants with markets. The system did not abolish rural credit or replace agriculture with pastoralism.

s: Who helped Akbar introduce the Ain-i-Dahsala along with Muzaffar Khan Turbati?
x: Akbar introduced the Ain-i-Dahsala with the help of Khwaja Shah Mansoor and Muzaffar Khan Turbati.

s: Under the zabt system, what was the 'patta' given to the peasant?
x: Patta was the title deed; the deed of agreement given by the peasant was the qabuliyat.

s: In the zabt system, what was the 'qabuliyat'?
x: Qabuliyat was the deed of agreement, while patta was the title deed.

s: The major source of the silver that reached India through European trade was the silver of which region?
x: Much of the silver came from Spanish America in the New World and reached India through Europe and the Pacific.

s: What was one effect of the inflow of silver into Mughal India?
o: The disappearance of bullion from markets
x: The silver influx increased silver rupee coinage and raised prices.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding British trade policy in India?
o: Indian exports received preferential treatment in Britain.
The policy harmed Indian handicraft industries.
Indian exports were heavily charged in Britain.
x: Option A is incorrect: Indian exports were heavily taxed in Britain, while British goods entering India got preferential treatment. That one-sided policy ruined Indian handicraft industries.

s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of goods exported from Mughal India?
o: War horses, silver, porcelain and wine
x: Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar were all exports of Mughal India. Each of the other groups contains imports such as watches, tin, ivory, glass, copper, war horses, silver, porcelain and wine.

s: The expression ‘sink of precious metals’ in the context of early modern India refers to which of the following?
o: India’s export of all its silver coinage to Europe
India’s absorption of large quantities of imported gold and silver
The use of silver only in royal karkhanas
The replacement of silver by copper currency
x: India became a ‘sink of precious metals’ because European companies paid for Indian goods with bullion, causing large inflows of gold and silver.

s: To whom did the Golden Firman issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah grant trade rights?
x: The Golden Firman issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda granted trade rights to the English.

s: Which of the following was an import into Mughal India?
x: War horses were imported; saltpetre, indigo and muslin were exports.

s: Which Mughal emperor's firman of 1716/1717 cut the duties of the English?
x: Farrukhsiyar's firman of 1716/1717 cut English duties.

s:
Consider the following statements about Indian Ocean commerce in the Mughal period:
1. Armenians were among the Asian merchant groups.
2. The trade balance favoured India till the mid-18th century.
3. Europeans paid for Indian goods mainly in bullion.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Armenians were among the Asian merchants, Europeans paid in bullion, and the trade balance favoured India till the mid-18th century.

s: Which of the following statements about eighteenth-century Bengal is incorrect?
x: Option D is incorrect: 18th-century Bengal exported cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium, not copper. Copper was one of the goods traded at Motupalli.

s: Who made up the Mughal nobility (umara)?
x: The nobility consisted of high mansabdars, drawn from Turanis, Iranis, Hindustanis and Rajputs.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Khud-kasht – cultivated land in the peasant's own village
Khud-kasht – cultivated land in another village
Pahi-kasht – cultivated land in the peasant's own village
Pahi-kasht – crown land of the emperor
x: Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village, whereas pahi-kasht peasants cultivated land in another village.

s: Besides private enterprises, in which state workshops did Mughal artisans work?
x: Artisans worked in state karkhanas as well as private enterprises and were often organised in guilds.

s: In the Mughal period, what was a peasant who cultivated land in another village called?
x: Pahi-kasht cultivated land in another village; khud-kasht cultivated land in his own village.

s:
Consider the following statements about Mughal rural society:
1. Zamindars were hereditary holders of superior rights in rural land.
2. Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Zamindars were hereditary rural superior-right holders, and khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village.

s: What did Mughal karkhanas, continuing a Sultanate tradition, mainly produce?
x: Karkhanas made court luxury goods such as gold and silver articles, fine textiles, arms and jewellery.

s: Who supervised the Mughal royal karkhanas?
x: The Mughal royal karkhanas were supervised by the Mir Saman, also known as Khan-i-Saman.

s: Which of the following was NOT a typical product of the Mughal karkhanas?
x: The karkhanas made court luxuries such as gold and silver articles, fine textiles, carpets, arms and jewellery, not bulk grain.

s: Who built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra?
x: Nur Jahan built Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb.

s: What did Jahanara, Shah Jahan's daughter and Padshah Begum, build?
o: The Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk
The Moti Masjid in Agra Fort
x: Jahanara built the Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk. The Agra Fort Moti Masjid was Shah Jahan's and Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb was built by Nur Jahan.

s: Who contrasted the strict veiling of Muslim women with the freer movement of Hindu women in A New Account of East India and Persia?
x: John Fryer described this contrast for the Deccan in A New Account of East India and Persia.

s: Bernier and Tavernier reported the prevalence of which practices in Mughal India?
o: Abolition of sati and widow remarriage
Widow remarriage, monogamy and late marriage
x: Bernier and Tavernier referred to the prevalence of sati, child marriage and polygamy, though Akbar tried to stop forced sati.

s: In the Mughal period, what was property controlled by Hindu women known as?
x: Hindu women controlled stridhana; Muslim women had inheritance shares and mehr under sharia.

s: Who wrote the Humayun-nama?
x: Gulbadan Begum, Babur's daughter, wrote the Humayun-nama.

s: Whose daughter was Zeb-un-Nissa, who wrote poetry under the pen name 'Makhfi'?
x: Zeb-un-Nissa was Aurangzeb's daughter and wrote under the pen name Makhfi.

s: Under sharia, besides inheritance shares, what right did Muslim women have in the Mughal period?
x: Muslim women had inheritance shares and mehr; stridhana was the property of Hindu women.

s: In which year did Nur Jahan marry Jahangir?
x: Nur Jahan married Jahangir in 1611.

s: Who was the only Mughal empress whose name appeared on coins?
x: Nur Jahan's name appeared on coins and farmans; she was the only empress so named on coins.

s: Which social practice did Akbar try to stop?
x: Akbar tried to stop forced sati; Bernier and Tavernier reported sati in Mughal India.

s: Bernier’s observation about the urban society of Delhi was that it
o: had no real middle class, with people tending to be either very rich or very poor
was dominated by peasants who had migrated from villages
had a large and prosperous middle class between the rich and poor
consisted entirely of artisans employed by the state
x: Bernier found no real middle class in Delhi and described a sharp contrast between the very rich and the very poor.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mughal urban society?
o: Artisans worked both in state karkhanas and privately.
Artisans were often organised in guilds.
Urban society consisted of merchants and soldiers only.
Physicians, teachers and lawyers formed professional groups.
x: Urban society was not made up only of merchants and soldiers; it also included artisans and professional groups.

s: Who founded the Dars-e-Nizami?
x: Mulla Nizamuddin of Sihali, linked with Firangi Mahal, Lucknow, founded the Dars-e-Nizami.

s: For what was Firangi Mahal at Lucknow noted as a madrasa?
x: Firangi Mahal in Lucknow was a madrasa associated with Muslim jurisprudence.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mughal court customs?
o: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Shah Jahan.
Jharokha darshan was begun by Akbar and ended by Aurangzeb.
Tuladan weighed the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday.
Nauroz was a Persian New Year festival adopted from the Zoroastrians.
x: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Akbar, not Shah Jahan.

s: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, by what name was Muharram popularly known?
x: Muharram was known as Peerla Panduga in Golconda.

s: Who began the Mughal custom of jharokha darshan?
x: Jharokha darshan was begun by Akbar and ended by Aurangzeb.

s: What did Tuladan, adopted by Akbar, involve?
o: Weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday
The emperor appearing daily at a balcony
x: Tuladan, a Hindu custom, weighed the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday for gifts to the poor.

s: Which Mughal emperor abolished the Nauroz court festival?
x: Nauroz, the Persian New Year, was made a court festival by Akbar and abolished by Aurangzeb.

s: Nauroz, made a Mughal court festival by Akbar, was the New Year festival of which tradition?
x: Nauroz is the Persian New Year; Akbar made it a court festival and Aurangzeb abolished it.

s: Tuladan, adopted by Akbar, was originally a custom of which tradition?
x: Tuladan, weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday, was a Hindu custom adopted by Akbar.

s: Which traveller contrasted the luxury of Mughal nobles with the misery of servants and workmen?
x: Pelsaert, the Dutch factor, contrasted nobles' luxury with the misery of servants and workmen.

s:
Consider the following statements about slavery in Mughal India:
1. Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war.
2. After Akbar's measure, slaves disappeared from noble households.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Akbar stopped enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562, yet noble households remained full of slaves and large domestic staffs.

s: Which Mughal emperor stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war?
x: Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562.

s: Which measure did Akbar take in 1562?
o: Stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war
x: In 1562 Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war. Jizya was abolished in 1564, the pilgrimage tax in 1563, and the Ibadat Khana was built in 1575.

s: In which year did Akbar abolish the jizya?
x: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564, after abolishing the pilgrimage tax in 1563.

s: What did Mughal nobles, drawn from Turanis, Iranis, Afghans, Hindustanis, Rajputs and Deccanis, remain dependent on?
x: The nobles were wealthy but wholly dependent on the emperor's favour.

s: Which groups dominated the Mughal nobility under Babur and Humayun?
x: Turanis and Iranis dominated under Babur and Humayun; Akbar added Rajputs and Hindustanis, and Deccanis and Marathas grew under Aurangzeb.

s: Under Akbar, which groups were added to the Mughal nobility to balance the Turanis and Iranis?
x: Akbar added Rajputs and Hindustanis to balance the Turanis and Iranis.

s: According to M. Athar Ali, what was the Hindu share of the nobility under Aurangzeb?
x: After the Deccan wars Deccanis and Marathas swelled the nobility, and the Hindu share was about one-third.

s: Who were referred to as 'Hindustanis' in the Mughal nobility?
x: Hindustanis were Indian Muslims; Turanis were Central Asians and Iranis Persians.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Khud-kasht – cultivator of land in another village
Muzarian – tenant cultivating land held by another person
Pahi-kasht – resident peasant cultivating his own village land
Muzarian – resident peasant cultivating his own land
x: Muzarian were tenants who cultivated land held by others. Khud-kasht were resident cultivators, while pahi-kasht cultivated land in another village.

s: A khud-kasht peasant in Mughal India was one who:
o: Was a tenant of a zamindar
Cultivated land in his own village
x: Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village; pahi-kasht cultivated in another village.

s: Who were the 'muzarian' in the Mughal period?
o: Owners of land in their own village
Tenants cultivating land held by others
x: Muzarian were tenants who cultivated land held by others, not owners.

s: Niccolao Manucci served at the Mughal court first as an artilleryman and later as what?
x: Manucci, a Venetian, was an artilleryman and later a physician; he wrote Storia do Mogor.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Peter Mundy – Physician of Dara Shikoh
x: Pelsaert, the Dutch factor, wrote Remonstrantie. Bernier was Dara Shikoh's physician, Tavernier the diamond merchant and Mundy an English traveller.
